query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In steels for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, corrosion resistance is enhanced by a mechanism in which manganese preferentially dissolves—due to its lower tendency to form stable fluorides—than chromium. This preferential Mn dissolution maintains a chromium-enriched surface that forms a stable, protective oxide (or hydroxide) layer that impedes further corrosive attack.
generation.material_initial_state: Steels with similar chromium content (e.g., ~18 wt.% Cr as in 316H stainless steel) but differing in manganese content (a standard low-Mn variant versus an Mn-enhanced formulation).
generation.intervention: Expose the steels to a controlled aggressive environment such as molten fluoride salt (or an analogous chemical-processing fluid) at operating temperatures typical of nuclear or chemical processing units (e.g., 700–800 °C) for a set duration.
generation.conditions: A well-controlled environment with fixed temperature, salt composition (including controlled levels of impurities like moisture), and exposure time to ensure reproducibility. Post-exposure, samples should be cooled under inert conditions to preserve surface chemistry.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, chromium-enriched protective layer (oxide/hydroxide scale) on the steel’s surface that arises from reduced chromium dissolution as manganese dissolves preferentially.
generation.mechanism: Because manganese forms its fluoride with a lower standard Gibbs free energy compared to chromium, Mn is more readily dissolved into the salt. This selective dissolution limits the loss of chromium, which remains to form a compact, self-healing protective layer that acts as a diffusion barrier to further corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel variants with enhanced Mn content will exhibit lower net Cr loss, formation of a more robust chromium-enriched surface layer, and overall reduced mass loss compared to the baseline (low-Mn) steel when measured by spectroscopic surface analysis and gravimetric methods.
generation.baseline: Conventional 316H stainless steel (approximately 2 wt.% Mn) that, under the same conditions, shows higher rates of chromium dissolution and greater overall corrosion (mass loss, thinner or less protective oxide scale).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid in molten fluoride salt environments (or similarly aggressive chemical-processing conditions) encountered in nuclear power and chemical industries. The hypothesis may not hold in environments dominated by different corrosion mechanisms (e.g., high-pressure steam oxidation).
generation.uncertainty: While a directional trend (Mn-enhanced steels resisting Cr dissolution better) is anticipated, the precise quantitative differences in dissolution rates, oxide scale formation, and long‐term stability remain uncertain. Additionally, impurity levels in the salt and minor alloying variations may influence the observed effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of steels with the same chromium content but differing manganese levels (standard low-Mn versus Mn-enhanced). Subject all samples to identical exposure in a molten fluoride salt bath at a constant temperature (e.g., 750 °C) for a predetermined time. Periodically remove samples for post-exposure analysis.
measurements: Mass change (gravimetric analysis) before and after exposure
Elemental composition at the surface and in the bulk (using techniques such as ICP-MS, XPS, or EDS) to track Cr and Mn concentrations
Characterization of the surface oxide/hydroxide layer (using SEM, TEM, or XRD) to assess thickness and compositional uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn-enhanced steels do not demonstrate a significantly lower rate of Cr loss or fail to develop a markedly more protective Cr-enriched layer compared to the low-Mn steels—or if both variants show similar corrosion behavior—the hypothesis that preferential Mn dissolution governs corrosion resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion behavior

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy [2] . Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion [2] .
